label: When You Are Afraid
framing: Scripture says do not be afraid again and again, and it is never spoken to deny the danger. It is spoken because of who stands beside you in the danger, the God who promises his presence on the very ground that frightens you most.
cultural: Joshua was told to be strong and courageous as he faced armies and an unknown land with Moses newly dead. The fishermen Jesus called knew the terror of a storm on the Sea of Galilee, and the early church heard fear not as you will be spared but as I am with you when you are not. Courage in the Bible is never the absence of fear.
historical: The martyrs of the early church walked toward death singing, not because they felt no fear but because they trusted a presence stronger than it. Across the centuries, from Polycarp in the second century to Dietrich Bonhoeffer facing the gallows in 1945, believers have located courage not in their own nerve but in the God who does not abandon his people.
application: Name the fear plainly rather than letting it run unspoken in the dark. Take the next faithful step even while afraid, since courage is fear that has prayed and moved anyway. Surround yourself with people who steady you. And anchor your mind on the promise of God's presence rather than on the size of the threat, returning to it as often as the fear returns.

verses.text: Now this is what the LORD says— He who created you, O Jacob, and He who formed you, O Israel: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine! When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze.
verses.where: God tells Israel not to fear, and gives his reasons: he created them, redeemed them, called them by name, and will be with them through water and fire. The site's note on the chapter lists those reasons in that order. The promise is not that there will be no rivers to cross, but that they will not cross them alone.

verses.text: The LORD is my light and my salvation— whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life— whom shall I dread?
verses.where: David asks whom he shall fear, with the LORD as his light, salvation and stronghold. The site's plain note says the question is asked because there is something to fear, and that the same man prays in anguish later in the psalm. Courage in the Bible, it says, is not the absence of fear; it is trust that holds when fear is present.

verses.text: After these events, the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: “Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward.”
verses.where: After Abram has defeated four kings, made enemies in the east and refused Sodom's wealth, God tells him not to be afraid: I am your shield, your very great reward. The site's note says God speaks to both fears, protection and provision. The plain note adds that when Abram brought God his honest worry, God did not scold him but took him outside to see the stars.

verses.text: But Moses told the people, “Do not be afraid. Stand firm and you will see the LORD’s salvation, which He will accomplish for you today; for the Egyptians you see today, you will never see again. The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still.”
verses.where: Trapped between Pharaoh's chariots and the sea, the people panic, and Moses tells them not to be afraid but to stand firm and see the LORD's salvation; the LORD will fight for them. The site's note on the chapter tells how the sea was divided and they crossed on dry ground. Fear here is answered not by a plan but by a promise, and the people are asked to be still before they are asked to walk.

verses.text: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.
verses.where: The shepherd's psalm walks through the valley of the shadow of death and fears no evil, for you are with me. The site's plain note says the promise is not that the sheep will never be in danger, but that the shepherd will never leave, and that the comfort of verse 4 is not you will not go into the valley but you are with me in it.

verses.text: I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears.
verses.where: David says he sought the LORD, who answered him and delivered him from all his fears. The site's plain note points out where he learned it: not in a palace, but pretending to be mad in an enemy city. Deliverance from fear came to a frightened man in a humiliating place.

verses.text: Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father. And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.
verses.where: Sending his disciples out to face rejection, Jesus tells them not to fear, because sparrows, the cheapest food in the market, do not fall apart from their Father, and the hairs of their head are numbered. The site's note says the argument moves from the least to the greater. The plain note asks the reader to name something they are afraid of and put it beside the sparrow.

verses.text: He could see that the disciples were straining to row, because the wind was against them. About the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them, but when they saw Him walking on the sea, they cried out, thinking He was a ghost— for they all saw Him and were terrified. But Jesus spoke up at once: “Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.”
verses.where: The disciples are straining at the oars against the wind in the night, and when they see Jesus walking on the sea they cry out in terror. He speaks at once: take courage, it is I, do not be afraid. The site's note says the words of comfort are also words of revelation, and the plain note says that Jesus saw them straining while he was far away on the mountain, though they did not know he saw.

verses.text: He took with Him Peter, James, and John, and began to be deeply troubled and distressed. Then He said to them, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” Going a little farther, He fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour would pass from Him. “Abba, Father,” He said, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.”
verses.where: In Gethsemane Jesus is deeply troubled and distressed, says his soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death, and prays that the cup be taken from him, yet not what I will. The site's plain note says he felt horror at death as a real man would, and freely gave his will to the Father's. Fear is not sin; Jesus himself was afraid, and he said so to his friends and to his Father.

verses.text: When I saw Him, I fell at His feet like a dead man. But He placed His right hand on me and said, “Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last, the Living One. I was dead, and behold, now I am alive forever and ever! And I hold the keys of Death and of Hades.
verses.where: On Patmos John sees the glorified Son of Man and falls at his feet like a dead man. The risen Christ places his right hand on him and says do not be afraid: he was dead and is alive forever, and he holds the keys of Death and of Hades. In the Bible's last book the risen Christ says to a terrified man what the angel said to the shepherds at his birth (Luke 2:10): do not be afraid.

misread.taken: God has not given us a spirit of fear is used to tell anxious or frightened Christians that their fear proves weak faith, or that it does not come from God and so should simply stop.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Paul is speaking to Timothy about courage in his work, not shrinking back from the gospel or from a friend in chains. He is not saying that anyone who feels fear has a weak faith; Paul himself admits to sorrow and to being anxious. The verse points a fearful person to what God gives and does not shame them for being afraid, and it is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in the verse forbids it.
misread.text: For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

whole: Fear comes in many sizes. A scan result not yet back. A child out late with the roads icy. A court date, a layoff rumor, a lump, a letter from the bank. Some fears are sudden and sharp; others have been living in the chest so long they feel like part of the furniture. Christians often carry an extra weight on top of the fear itself: the sense that a person with real faith would not be afraid, so the fear must also be a spiritual failure. They pray, and the fear does not leave, and they conclude something is wrong with them. If fear has become constant, wakes you at night, or brings panic you cannot stop, it is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.

Scripture says do not be afraid again and again, and it says it to people in real danger. It says it to Abram after a battle, to a people trapped against the sea, to disciples straining at the oars in the dark, to John lying at the feet of the risen Christ. The Bible does not treat fear as shameful. David asks whom he shall fear and then prays in anguish a few verses later. Jesus in Gethsemane was deeply distressed and said so. The real danger the Bible names is not feeling afraid but letting fear decide: hiding what God has given, refusing what he asks, or trusting only what we can control. Most of us know that pull. We plan, check and rehearse, and the fear grows because we have made ourselves the only one standing between us and the thing we dread.

So the Bible's wisdom answers fear not with a technique but with a person. Do not fear, God says, and almost always gives a reason: I have redeemed you, I am your shield, I am with you, it is I. When you are afraid, David says, put your trust in God; the fear comes first, and trust is what you do with it. Tell God plainly what you are afraid of, as Jesus did in the garden, and tell someone near you too. Ask for what you need and leave room for the Father's will. Remember what God has already done, the way Israel remembered the sea. And take the next step that is yours to take, even shaking; courage in Scripture is trust that holds while the fear is still there.

The hope Scripture gives is that the one who says do not be afraid has gone through the worst thing himself. Jesus was afraid in Gethsemane, went to the cross, and rose, and now he holds the keys of Death and of Hades. The shepherd does not promise there will be no valley; he promises to be in it. Not one sparrow falls apart from your Father, and you are worth more than many sparrows. Fear may still come tomorrow. It does not get the last word.
deep.sit: What are you most afraid of right now, and what would it change to say it out loud to God, and to one person you trust, this week?

prayer.lead: A prayer of someone hounded and afraid. The site's plain note says verse 3 does not say I am never afraid; it says when I am afraid. Fear comes. Trust is what you do with it.
prayer.text: When I am afraid, I put my trust in You. In God, whose word I praise— in God I trust. I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?

careLines.text: Getting help is not a lack of faith, and nothing in this verse forbids it.
Lost sleep and heavy thoughts are worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a failure of faith.
